cultivar: Regional landraces and standard clones; not cultivar-specific
processing: Pan-fired ('chao qing') green: mature leaf is fired, rolled into fine twists and dried in rotating pans or drums until it curls into the long, slightly bent 'eyebrow' shape; machine-made as a commodity grade.
harvest_season: Spring through autumn, blended; not sold by picking date.
appearance_dry: Thin, tightly twisted, slightly curved leaves like eyebrows, dull dark green to grey-green.
appearance_wet: Even, mid-sized olive leaves, fairly whole in the higher grades.
taste_profile: Dry, plummy and faintly tart with toasted-grain roastiness and a lightly smoky edge; brisk and thin rather than lush.

brewing.notes: Western-style, 80–85 °C, two to three minutes. It is the tea of choice for Moroccan and Central Asian sweet mint tea, where it is boiled; brewed gently on its own it is a plain, slightly acidic daily green.

vintage_note: Sold year-round as a graded export commodity, with no harvest date and no vintage; trade grades are numbered (41022 is the classic top grade, with 9371, 8147 and others below it) and the tea is blended for consistency. It is the staple green of much of North Africa, Central Asia and the Arab world. Stored sealed it keeps a year or more; freshness matters less than with famous greens.
description:
Chun Mee is the export green you have probably drunk without knowing it: the plain, twisted-leaf 'eyebrow' tea that fills supermarket boxes in Morocco, Algeria, Uzbekistan and the Gulf, and the base of countless sweet mint teas. The name is Cantonese-flavoured trade English for zhen mei, 'precious eyebrows', after the curved shape of the leaf. Wuyuan in Jiangxi was the historic source; Zhejiang and Anhui make a great deal of it too.

It is a fully pan-fired green ('chao qing'), made from leaf picked bigger and later than any famous tea, rolled into tight twists and dried in rotating pans so that it curls. The point of the style is a sturdy, tightly rolled leaf that stores and ships well and tastes consistent from year to year, so it is blended and graded by number rather than tied to a garden or a date.

The cup is dry and brisk, with toasted grain, a plummy, slightly tart fruitiness and a hint of smoke; thin, but it holds sugar and mint well, which is exactly what its main customers want. On its own, brew it at 80–85 °C for a couple of minutes in a pot. Boiling water and long steeps are fine if you are adding mint and sugar; they are not fine if you are drinking it plain.

Buying is simple: look for the grade. The classic top grade is numbered 41022, with 9371 and others below; higher grades have finer, more even twists and fewer stalks. Pricier 'Moon Palace' or 'special' Chun Mee from Western retailers is usually a higher grade of the same thing rather than a different tea. Do not pay for a vintage or a mountain name here; they do not apply.

It is also a good tea for learning: taste it against a Hyson and a gunpowder and you will have covered the three classic Chinese export green shapes in one sitting.
sources_note: Grade numbers follow the usual export numbering (41022 as the top grade); minor codes vary between exporters.
